_readme: Short, self-contained information sheets for a document-RAG strategy over Park Guell and Casa Mila (La Pedrera), covering both monuments and their notable elements. Unlike data/graphs/demo_personas.json, cross-monument connections are NOT modeled as shared 'technique' nodes -- each sheet instead carries a 'similarities' field with short, inline cross-references so a single retrieved chunk stays self-contained. 'general_knowledge_facts' are facts not stated verbatim in the cited local articles; they are common art/architecture-history knowledge or explicitly flagged as disputed/popular interpretation, and should be treated with slightly lower confidence than 'artistic_facts'/'technical_facts'. Every sheet lists its own 'sources'; see the top-level 'sources' block for full citations.

sheets.name: Park Güell
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí, commissioned by Eusebi Güell
sheets.timeline: Commissioned 1900 as a private residential development; built 1900-1914 (works abandoned with only 2 of 60 planned houses built); sold by Güell's heirs to Barcelona City Council in 1922; opened as a municipal park in 1926; declared an artistic monument in 1969; UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984.
sheets.inspiration: Inspired by the English garden-city movement (hence the English word 'Park' in its name); marks Gaudí's 'naturalist period', in which his study of nature and organic forms drove both ornament and underlying structural geometry. Symbolic references throughout include political Catalanism (entrance stairway) and Catholicism (the Calvary, originally conceived as a chapel).
sheets.construction_process: Built 1900-1914 as a failed private residential estate (60 triangular plots planned, only 2 houses built) before being abandoned and later purchased by the City Council.
technical_facts: Uses inverted catenary arches for its viaducts and elevated pathways, the same load-bearing-compression method Gaudí used earlier at Colònia Güell.
Entry to the Monumental Zone (main terrace, mosaics, viaducts, gate area) has required a paid ticket since October 2013; Barcelona residents enter free.
artistic_facts: UNESCO's 1984 inscription describes the park's architecture as combining the Arts and Crafts movement, Symbolism, Expressionism, and Rationalism, and as having presaged techniques of 20th-century Modernism.
Introduced curved, undulating benches at Park Güell -- a precursor to the style Gaudí later fully realized at the Sagrada Família.
similarities: Same architect (Antoni Gaudí) and same 1984 UNESCO 'Works of Antoni Gaudí' listing as la_pedrera.
Catenary/compression structural logic shared with catenaria_pedrera, though executed in stone viaducts here versus brick vaulting there.

sheets.name: El Drac (Dragon / Salamander)
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Built as part of the main terrace/entrance works, documented as complete by the January 1903 Anuari de l'Associació d'Arquitectes description of the site.
sheets.inspiration: Popularly associated with mythological guardian-dragon imagery, though sources disagree on whether the figure represents a dragon or a salamander -- the official park site itself uses both terms.
sheets.construction_process: A curved masonry/mortar core was built up first, then clad in small, irregular ceramic trencadís fragments (rather than flat tiles) so the mosaic skin could conform to the compound curvature without cracking.
technical_facts: Functions as the overflow spout of the park's rainwater system: water falling on the Greek Theatre/Nature Square above is collected by a conduit inside the Hypostyle Room's colonnade and channeled to an underground cistern, with the dragon's mouth as that system's overflow outlet.
artistic_facts: Covered in trencadís (tile-shard mosaic); the official park site calls it 'the most popular image of the park.'
Sits on the Dragon Stairway, a twin flight of steps divided into three landings: goblin-like shapes on the first landing, the emblem of Catalonia on the second, and the dragon/salamander further up.
general_knowledge_facts: Popularly associated with mythological guardian-dragon imagery (e.g. the dragon of the Garden of the Hesperides) -- a widely repeated interpretation, not confirmed by any Gaudí-authored source.
similarities: Trencadís cladding technique shared with caps_pedrera (La Pedrera's chimneys) and banc_serpentejant (the serpentine bench, same park).

sheets.name: Pòrtic de la Bugaderia (Laundry Room Portico / Washerwoman's Portico)
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Part of the original park infrastructure built 1900-1914.
sheets.inspiration: Described by the park's own site as taking 'the shape of a great wave atop slanting columns' -- called one of the finest examples of Gaudí's organic architecture; the slanted double colonnade evokes a stone forest, echoing how the park's viaduct columns and vaults elsewhere mimic tree trunks and natural forms.
sheets.construction_process: Built from unworked stone taken from the same hillside it stands on, so the structure visually grows out of the mountain rather than sitting on top of it.
technical_facts: The double colonnade of slanting columns acts as a structural buttress against the retaining wall behind it -- the tilt is load-bearing, not decorative.

Uses the same structural logic as the park's viaducts: inclined stone columns form a parabola/inverted-catenary profile so the columns work in pure compression along the line of thrust, without needing external buttressing.
similarities: Shares its inclined-column, inverted-catenary compression logic with viaductes_park_guell (same park) and, in brick-vault form, with catenaria_pedrera (La Pedrera's attic).

sheets.name: Porter's Lodge (entrance gatehouses)
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Built early in the 1900-1914 construction phase; documented as already constructed by the January 1903 Anuari de l'Associació d'Arquitectes description.
sheets.inspiration: Whimsical, fairy-tale-like pavilion forms marking the park's main entrance, reflecting Güell's ambition to recreate an English residential-park model.
technical_facts: One of the two pavilions originally housed a phone booth; the other now contains a permanent exhibit of the Barcelona City History Museum.
artistic_facts: Forms a pair of gatehouses flanking the park's main entrance, among the first structures built on site.

sheets.name: Serpentine Bench (Banc de trencadís)
sheets.creator: Josep Maria Jujol (design of the trencadís bench, under Gaudí's overall project)
sheets.timeline: Built as part of the main terrace works during the 1900-1914 construction phase; the terrace and its hypostyle support were already in use for events by 1907.
sheets.inspiration: Its ergonomic, curving form creates enclaves along its length that encourage social interaction rather than facing visitors outward in a straight line.
sheets.construction_process: Long, curving bench shaped like a sea serpent, bordering the terrace above the Hypostyle Room, clad in trencadís mosaic.
technical_facts: Sits directly atop the Hypostyle Room's vaulted terrace, following the ergonomic curve designed to double as a shared social space rather than a simple boundary wall.
artistic_facts: One of Gaudí's introductions of curved, undulating bench forms at Park Güell, a precursor to the style he later fully realized at the Sagrada Família.
similarities: Trencadís technique shared with drac_park_guell (same park) and caps_pedrera (La Pedrera's chimneys).
Design attributed to Jujol, like the interior wrought-iron gate at patis_pedrera (La Pedrera).

sheets.name: Hypostyle Room (Room of a Hundred Columns)
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Documented as fully covered/completed by 1907, when events were already being held in the great square above it; the tiled bench that borders the terrace above was completed in 1914.
sheets.inspiration: The vaulted colonnade's mosaic-decorated ceiling recalls grotesque motifs inspired by Roman architecture, particularly the Domus Aurea.
sheets.construction_process: A forest of columns forming a vaulted space that structurally supports the great terrace and serpentine bench above it.
technical_facts: Functions as part of the park's rainwater collection system: a conduit inside the colonnade gathers water falling on the terrace above and channels it to an underground cistern, ultimately overflowing through the dragon's mouth (see drac_park_guell).
artistic_facts: Ceiling mosaics recall grotesque motifs inspired by Roman architecture, particularly the Domus Aurea.
similarities: Structurally supports banc_serpentejant (the terrace bench above) and feeds the water system that exits through drac_park_guell.

sheets.name: Viaducts / elevated pathways
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Built during the 1900-1914 construction phase; documented as partly complete (viaducts and part of the great esplanade) by the January 1903 Anuari de l'Associació d'Arquitectes description.
sheets.inspiration: Columns and vaulted supports mimic tree trunks and natural forms, blending the paths seamlessly with the surrounding landscape.
sheets.construction_process: A system of elevated pathways, originally intended for carriages, built from local stone using inclined columns and vaulted supports that follow the natural lie of the land.
technical_facts: As with Gaudí's earlier work at Colònia Güell, the viaducts use inverted catenary arches to achieve optimal load-bearing compression, so the stone columns work in pure compression without needing external buttressing.
artistic_facts: Columns and vaulted supports mimic tree trunks and natural forms, part of Gaudí's naturalist-period design language for the park.
similarities: Shares its inclined-column, inverted-catenary compression logic with porxada_bugaderia (same park) and, in brick-vault form, with catenaria_pedrera (La Pedrera's attic).

sheets.name: Casa Milà (La Pedrera)
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí, commissioned by Pere Milà and Roser Segimon
sheets.timeline: Commissioned September 1905; presented to Barcelona City Council February 1906; pre-existing building demolished and construction begun 1906; completed December 1910; certificate of completion issued October 1912; declared a historic/artistic monument in 1969; UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984; headquarters of Fundació Catalunya La Pedrera since 2013.

technical_figures.stories: 9 (basement, ground floor, mezzanine, main/noble floor, four upper floors, attic)

sheets.inspiration: Gaudí designed the house as 'a constant curve, both outside and inside,' combining ruled geometry with naturalistic form. There is no agreement on which mountain inspired the facade -- candidates proposed by different contemporaries include the rocks of Fray Guerau in the Prades mountains, St. Miquel del Fai, the Torrent de Pareis cliffs in Menorca, Uçhisar in Cappadocia, and Mola Gallifa.
materials: limestone (Garraf Massif, lower floor; Villefranche quarry, upper floors)
sheets.construction_process: Gaudí's last private residence commission; the pre-existing building on the plot was demolished (unlike the Casa Batlló renovation) and the new self-supporting stone facade, connected to curved iron floor beams, was built 1906-1910.
technical_facts: Self-supporting stone facade with no load-bearing walls, connected to curved iron beams surrounding the perimeter of each floor -- allowing interior walls to be added or removed without affecting the building's stability.

In August 1908 the City Council fined the project for exceeding its permitted height and site boundaries; the dispute was resolved in December 1909 when the building was certified as monumental and exempted from strict bylaw compliance.
artistic_facts: Nicknamed 'La Pedrera' ('the stone quarry') by residents who disliked its rough-hewn, undulating stone facade -- an insult that became its popular name.
Considered a predecessor of later biomorphic buildings such as the 1921 Einstein Tower (Erich Mendelsohn), the Guggenheim Museum (Frank Wright), and Frank Gehry's Disney Concert Hall.
similarities: Same architect (Antoni Gaudí) and same 1984 UNESCO 'Works of Antoni Gaudí' listing as park_guell.
Catenary/compression structural logic shared with park_guell's viaducts and pòrtic, though executed as brick vaulting here (see catenaria_pedrera) versus stone columns there.

sheets.name: Espai Gaudí attic (catenary/parabolic brick arches)
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí (arches marked on site by builder Bayó and foreman Canaleta)
sheets.timeline: Built during the main 1906-1910 construction phase, as the attic laundry/drying space beneath the roof.
sheets.inspiration: The rippling roofline is widely compared to the ribs of a huge animal or the fronds of a palm; the space, now called Espai Gaudí, is often described as feeling like walking through the inside of a whale's ribcage.
sheets.construction_process: Each arch's profile was set on site with a hanging-chain (catenary) model: nails were driven at the two spring points of the arch, a chain hung between them so its lowest point matched the desired deflection, and that traced curve became the template for the brick vault -- the same method Gaudí used at Casa Batlló and, earlier, on the roof of the Mataró workers' cooperative ('L'Obrera Mataronense').
technical_facts: Built using volta catalana (Catalan/timbrel vault) technique -- thin layered brick vaulting imported from Italy in the 14th century, laid without a full wooden centering framework.

Arch height and spacing directly follow the courtyards' footprint below: arches rise higher where the plan narrows and drop lower where it widens, so the roof structure encloses the irregular figure-8 courtyard shape beneath it.
artistic_facts: 270 parabolic brick arches of varying height, spaced about 80 cm apart, give the roofline a rippling, organic silhouette.
similarities: Same catenary/inverted-arch compression principle as park_guell's viaductes_park_guell and porxada_bugaderia, executed here in brick vaulting rather than stone columns.

sheets.name: Chimneys and rooftop sculptures ('caps')
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Built as part of the roof during the main 1906-1910 construction phase; later restored to remove post-Gaudí chimneys, TV antennas, and other later additions.
sheets.inspiration: Nicknamed the 'garden of warriors' by poet Pere Gimferrer, since the grouped chimneys look like helmeted sentinels standing guard over the skylight/staircase exits; their helmet-like silhouettes are sometimes linked to Gaudí's interest in medieval fortress architecture.
sheets.construction_process: Built from brick and coated with lime, broken marble, or glass; all pieces are functional (smoke extraction, ventilation, drainage) rather than purely decorative, despite their sculptural appearance.
technical_facts: The roof holds 28 chimneys in several groupings, 6 skylight/staircase exits, 2 half-hidden vents that renew air inside the building, and 4 discharge domes -- all functional rather than purely decorative.
Some staircase-exit towers double as housings for the building's water tanks, a few of which are snail-shaped.

The rooftop underwent a later restoration that removed chimneys added after Gaudí's death, TV antennas, and other additions, to return the roofscape closer to its originally designed functional layout.
artistic_facts: One chimney is topped with glass -- reportedly added by Gaudí the day after the building's inauguration party using empty champagne bottles, later restored with early-20th-century champagne-bottle bases.
similarities: Trencadís-style broken-tile cladding shared with drac_park_guell and banc_serpentejant (Park Güell).

sheets.name: Self-supporting stone facade
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Built during the main 1906-1910 construction phase; restored from 1987 onward, including rejoining fallen stone pieces sourced from the Villefranche quarry.
sheets.inspiration: Viewed from outside, the building reads in three parts: the main six-storey block with winding stone floors, two set-back floors with a smoother, whiter, wave-like curve, and the body of the roof.
sheets.construction_process: Large limestone blocks were cut to follow the projection of Gaudí's model, then raised into place and adjusted to align in a continuous curve with the surrounding pieces; the facade connects to curved iron floor beams rather than load-bearing walls.
technical_facts: Self-supporting: free of load-bearing walls, with the facade connected to curved iron beams around the perimeter of each floor, allowing large window openings and free interior layouts.
Original lower-level wrought ironwork was removed in 1928 when a tailor's shop opened in the building; one surviving balcony grille was later donated to MoMA, where it is on display.
artistic_facts: The undulating, rough-hewn stone facade and twisting wrought-iron balconies were controversial when built, giving rise to the 'La Pedrera' (stone quarry) nickname.
similarities: Structural principle (self-supporting facade, non-load-bearing) distinct from but complementary to catenaria_pedrera's compression-arch roof structure in the same building.

sheets.name: Courtyards and interior gate
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí (courtyard structure); wrought-iron gate design attributed to Josep Maria Jujol
sheets.timeline: Built during the main 1906-1910 construction phase.
sheets.inspiration: The floor-support beam structure was interpreted by Josep Maria Carandell, who built the centerpiece at a shipyard, as representing the helm of a ship -- 'the soul of the building,' with a resemblance to Gothic crypts. The iron entrance gate's non-symmetrical structure evokes soap bubbles formed between the hands, or the structure of a plant cell.
sheets.construction_process: Two courtyards (facing Passeig de Gràcia and Carrer de Provença) provide light to the building's nine stories; their floors are supported by cast-iron pillars, with two concentric cylindrical beams and stretched radial beams (like bicycle spokes) forming a central girder that works in tension and compression simultaneously.
technical_facts: The courtyard floor's central support girder combines two concentric cylindrical beams with stretched radial beams, functioning as a keystone working in both tension and compression -- structurally described as 'the soul of the building.'
The interior iron gate originally served both pedestrians and cars, providing access to the basement garage (now an auditorium).
artistic_facts: The two entrance halls are fully polychrome, with oil paintings on the plaster surfaces referencing mythology and flowers.
similarities: Wrought-iron gate design attributed to Jujol, like the trencadís serpentine bench (banc_serpentejant) at Park Güell.
